Paragraph: You are entitled to a right to carry out your tasks, but you’re in no position to enjoy the outcomes from your efforts. Don’t view yourself as the reason for the outcomes of your actions, and don’t let your inaction entangle you. This sloka highlights the importance of performing your duty without attachment to the results. It emphasizes the need to be free of things that matter and instead focus on performing one’s duties to the best of one’s ability.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Arjuna experiences performance anxiety, fear of failure, and paralysis of action due to deep worry about the consequences and outcomes of his choices in battle.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna introduces Nishkama Karma—instructing Arjuna to shift focus entirely onto the effort/process rather than obsessing over the results, avoiding both egoic ownership of outcomes and the trap of passive paralysis.
Outcome/Resolution: A path to psychological liberation and focus, allowing action to be taken with clarity, emotional equilibrium, and freedom from outcome-driven anxiety.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Anxiety: Performance anxiety, Fear of failure, Result obsession
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Work-Life Balance: Duty execution without burnout, Mindful effort

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Nishkama Karma (Desireless action performed without attachment to results)
Svadharma (Execution of personal duty aligned with one's inherent nature)
Anasakti (Mental detachment/dispassion toward fruits of action)
Samatvam (Equanimity of mind in success or failure)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: This verse articulates the cornerstone of Karma Yoga: human rights extend only to action, never to its fruits. True spiritual freedom arises when one releases egoistic ownership of results and avoids falling into passive apathy.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: A classic framework for reducing performance anxiety and burnout. Shifting internal locus of control away from unpredictable external outcomes toward controllable internal effort minimizes anticipatory anxiety and fosters task engagement.
